Strategic Research Synthesis: Competing Perspectives and Alternative Solution Paths in Industrial AI, Energy Optimization, and Advanced Scheduling
1. Executive Summary
This strategic research report synthesizes the competing paradigms, methodologies, and technological solution paths across the 31 scientific and technical documents in this knowledge base [1–31]. The literature addresses a critical industrial challenge: transforming heavy manufacturing—specifically steelmaking, continuous casting, reheating furnaces, hot/cold rolling mills, and heat treatment lines—from energy-intensive, inflexible operations into dynamic, sustainable, cyber-physical production systems.
Our synthesis reveals that the research community is divided into five distinct schools of thought (clusters), each advancing a fundamental philosophy to solve industrial scheduling, energy management, and control problems:
Exact Mathematical Programming & Optimal Control: Anchored in classical operations research and continuous control theory, emphasizing deterministic proofs, continuous dynamics, and exact or bounded competitive algorithms [1, 22–24, 28, 29, 31].
Evolutionary & Swarm Intelligence Metaheuristics: Focused on multi-objective trade-offs, fuzzy logic dominance, and surrogate-assisted search to navigate complex, high-dimensional combinatorial search spaces.
Cyber-Physical Digital Twins & IIoT Architectures: Centered on high-fidelity physical-virtual mapping, standardized Asset Administration Shells (AAS), and cross-process data integration to synchronize virtual plans with plant floor realities.
Deep Reinforcement Learning & Generative Industrial AI: Leveraging model-free sub-second online decision-making, multi-agent coordination, attention mechanisms, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), and Large Language Model (LLM) reward engineering for dynamic demand response.
Trustworthy Explainable AI & Human-Centric Industry 5.0: Prioritizing operator trust, process safety, intrinsic/post-hoc explainability, counterfactual recourse, and human-in-the-loop fatigue management.
2. Cluster Identification
Cluster 1: Exact Mathematical Programming & Optimal Control
Associated Documents: Benedikt et al., Gomes et al., Xu et al., Pena et al., Zhang et al., Liu et al., Hidri et al..
Core Concepts: Pontryagin's Minimum Principle, continuous bilinear furnace dynamics, concave idle energy functions, no-idle constraints, Benders' decomposition, robust optimization, deterministic competitive online algorithms, and rolling horizon MILP.
Main Technologies: Commercial MILP solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX), Shortest-path Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG), Continuous-time Optimal Control, and ARIMA / Holt-Winters forecasting engines.
Principal Authors or Contributors: O. Benedikt, P. Suca, Z. Hanzalek, A.C.L. Gomes, J. Xu, J.G.C. Pena, R. Zhang, L. Hidri.
Cluster 2: Evolutionary & Swarm Intelligence Metaheuristics

Core Concepts: Multi-objective Pareto optimization, surrogate-assisted fitness approximation (SVR/PSS), fuzzy logic dominance, open multi-objective traveling salesman problems (OMOTSP), and hybrid matheuristics.
Main Technologies: NSGA-II, Multi-Objective Particle Swarm Optimization (MOPSO), Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO), Enhanced Migrating Birds Optimization (EMBO), Back-Propagation Neural Networks (BPNN), and hyPDEVS simulation engines.
Principal Authors or Contributors: D. Wang, J. Long, F. Qiao, D. Han, Y. Duan, C. Rao, Q. Wang, L. Liu, T. Salhofer.
Cluster 3: Cyber-Physical Digital Twins & IIoT Architectures
Associated Documents: Li et al., Neuer et al., Javaid & Ullah, Li et al., Liu et al., Salhofer et al., Müller-Zhang et al..
Core Concepts: 5-Dimensional Digital Twin frameworks, Three-Stage Models (TSM) for logistics, IIoT "data continents", Asset Administration Shells (AAS), semantic ontologies, holonic virtual market auctions, and human smartwatch fatigue integration.
Main Technologies: BaSyx open-source AAS middleware, LightGBM, Three Population Algorithms (TPA), OPC-UA, cloud-edge computing architectures, and industrial wearable smartwatches.
Principal Authors or Contributors: S. Li, M. Neuer, W. Javaid, J. Li, Z. Müller-Zhang, T. Kuhn.

Associated Documents: Wang et al., Shah et al., Theumer et al., Zeng et al., Bashyal et al., Müller-Zhang et al..
Core Concepts: Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDP), Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) with ALADIN distributed optimization, Multi-Agent DRL (MADRL) with Centralized Training Decentralized Execution (CTDE), scaled dot-product attention, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), and LLM few-shot prompt reward design.
Main Technologies: PyTorch, Ray/RLlib, PettingZoo, OpenAI Gym / Gymnasium, Deep Q-Networks (DQN), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), and LLM ROSES prompting framework.
Principal Authors or Contributors: Z. Wang, M. Shah, P. Theumer, Y. Zeng, A. Bashyal, Z. Müller-Zhang.

Associated Documents: Wang & Chen, Morandini et al., Mehdiyev et al., Theumer et al., Javaid & Ullah, Arunthavanathan et al..
Core Concepts: Intrinsic vs. post-hoc explainability, decision tree rule extraction for evolutionary algorithms, SHAP and LIME feature attributions, system-level multi-objective counterfactual recourse, Intelligence Augmentation (IA), and Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA) process safety governance.
Main Technologies: Decision trees, SHAP, LIME, process mining operation logs, Assessment List for Trustworthy AI (ALTAI), and smartwatch physiological tracking.
Principal Authors or Contributors: Y. Wang, T. Chen, S. Morandini, N. Mehdiyev, P. Theumer, R. Arunthavanathan, W. Javaid.
3. Detailed Cluster Analysis
3.1 Cluster 1: Exact Mathematical Programming & Optimal Control
3.1.1 Fundamental Philosophy
Grounded in classical operations research and control theory, this philosophy asserts that physical manufacturing systems operate under deterministic physical laws that can be expressed through exact mathematical formulations. Proponents argue that approximations, metaheuristic random walks, or black-box neural networks introduce unacceptable operational risks, sub-optimality, or unproven bounds. The objective is to derive exact global optima, mathematically proven competitive ratios, or rigorous lower/upper bounds using control theory (such as Pontryagin's Minimum Principle) and mathematical programming.
3.1.2 Strengths
Provable Mathematical Guarantees: Delivers exact global optimal solutions or mathematically proven competitive ratios (e.g., competitive ratios of 1 + 1 / (B * alpha_min) or 1 + B * alpha_max for online furnace scheduling under thermal deterioration).
Physical Rigor: Incorporates true continuous system dynamics (such as bilinear heat loss equations or natural gas pipeline flow constraints) rather than oversimplified static mode graphs.
Strict Constraint Satisfaction: Hard operational constraints—such as no-idle furnace conditions, gas holder safety thresholds, and continuous casting no-wait rules—are guaranteed never to be violated.
3.1.3 Weaknesses
Exponential Computational Complexity: Exact MILP and Benders' decomposition approaches suffer from the combinatorial "curse of dimensionality" when scaling to industrial-sized plants, leading to excessive runtimes.
Rigidity to Unmodeled Stochasticity: Mathematical models require explicit parameterizations; unexpected real-time disruptions (e.g., sudden machine breakdowns or unpredicted weather shifts) can instantly render an exact schedule infeasible.
3.1.4 Opportunities
Hybrid Matheuristic Integration: Combining exact MILP sub-problem solvers with metaheuristic neighborhood searches to solve large-scale industrial instances in minutes.
Analytical Offline Pre-computation: Converting complex continuous control laws into offline concave energy functions that simplify online scheduling to simple shortest-path graph problems.
3.1.5 Risks
Execution Failure under Real-Time Disturbance: If plant floor execution deviates from modeled assumptions, rigid mathematical schedules cause operational bottlenecks or plant idling.
3.2 Cluster 2: Evolutionary & Swarm Intelligence Metaheuristics
3.2.1 Fundamental Philosophy
This school accepts that real-world manufacturing is inherently NP-hard, non-linear, multi-objective, and stochastic, rendering exact mathematical solvers impractical for large-scale real-time use. Instead of seeking guaranteed global optima at excessive computational cost, evolutionary computation uses nature-inspired population search mechanisms (crossover, mutation, swarm attraction, bird flocking) paired with surrogate fitness models or fuzzy logic to find high-quality Pareto-optimal trade-off solutions within acceptable timeframes.
3.2.2 Strengths
Multi-Objective Trade-Off Navigation: Naturally generates diverse Pareto frontiers, allowing decision-makers to evaluate explicit trade-offs between conflicting goals (e.g., gas consumption vs. job tardiness).
Robust Handling of Uncertainty: Integrates fuzzy logic membership functions and Support Vector Regression (SVR) surrogate evaluation to absorb random machine breakdowns, variable heating values, and processing delays.
High Scalability: Successfully handles massive industrial datasets (e.g., full hot strip mills or multi-stand rolling lines) where exact solvers fail to converge.
3.2.3 Weaknesses
Lack of Optimality Guarantees: Metaheuristics provide no mathematical proof of proximity to the true global optimum and can get trapped in local optima.
Parameter Sensitivity & Tuning Overhead: Performance relies heavily on fine-tuning population sizes, crossover/mutation rates, or swarm acceleration coefficients.
3.2.4 Opportunities
Simulation-Based Optimization: Utilizing discrete-event and hybrid continuous-discrete simulation engines as evaluators within evolutionary loops to capture complex physical system dynamics.
Data-Driven Surrogate Acceleration: Replacing computationally expensive Monte Carlo simulations with SVR or BPNN surrogate models to accelerate fitness evaluations by orders of magnitude.
3.2.5 Risks
Computation Sinks in High-Dimensional Search: Without surrogate assistance or problem-specific heuristic decoding, evolutionary search across thousands of slabs can stall or prove too slow for real-time dynamic rescheduling.
3.3 Cluster 3: Cyber-Physical Digital Twins & IIoT Architectures
3.3.1 Fundamental Philosophy
This approach posits that the primary bottleneck in industrial scheduling is not algorithm speed, but the information gap (data silos) between virtual planning models and physical shop-floor realities. Proponents contend that schedules fail because traditional MES/ERP systems lack real-time visibility into asset degradation, physical slab positions, and cross-process parameter heredity. By building 5-Dimensional Digital Twins connected via IIoT "data continents" and standardized Asset Administration Shells (AAS), optimization algorithms can execute closed-loop, live decision-making with high temporal and spatial fidelity.
3.3.2 Strengths
High-Fidelity Virtual Synchronization: Achieves slab position and charging/discharging time tracking in parallel walking beam furnaces with relative tracking errors below 0.98%.
Elimination of Cross-Process Data Silos: Connects upstream Hot Strip Rolling (HSR) data with downstream Cold Strip Rolling (CSR) via IIoT data platforms, raising thickness hit rates by 2% and reducing force fluctuations by over 50%.
Interoperability & Standardized Interfaces: Employs Asset Administration Shells (AAS) to enable plug-and-play communication between heterogeneous machinery, optimization engines, and wearable smartwatches.
3.3.3 Weaknesses
Massive Infrastructure & Capital Cost: Requires extensive deployment of IIoT sensor networks, edge-cloud computing layers, high-speed networks, and standardized digital thread software.
Model Maintenance & Drift: Digital Twin simulation models require constant re-calibration and maintenance to prevent physical-virtual divergence caused by equipment wear.
3.3.4 Opportunities
Human-Centric Industry 5.0 Integration: Ingesting smartwatch operator biometrics into Digital Twin models to track real-time worker fatigue and dynamically schedule microbreaks (Dynamic Break Integration).
Holonic Market Auctions: Deploying semantic product/order agents operating on virtual market structures to automatically re-allocate off-spec steel coils in sub-seconds.
3.3.5 Risks
Data Overload & Cyber-Physical Disconnect: If IIoT data pipelines experience latency, packet loss, or sensor drift, the Digital Twin will synchronize incorrect states, generating flawed production schedules.
3.4 Cluster 4: Deep Reinforcement Learning & Generative Industrial AI
3.4.1 Fundamental Philosophy
This school argues that both offline MILP and iterative metaheuristics are fundamentally unsuited for real-time, dynamic industrial demand response because their online computation times are too slow. DRL shifts the heavy computational burden offline—training artificial neural networks via environmental interaction—to enable sub-second online inference. By formulating industrial scheduling as Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDP) and leveraging advances like Multi-Agent PPO (MAPPO), attention mechanisms, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), and LLM reward engineering, DRL agents adapt instantly to volatile spot market electricity prices and renewable generation shifts.
3.4.2 Strengths
Sub-Second Online Decision Execution: Once policy networks are trained offline, online schedule execution occurs via feed-forward inference, running over 100 times faster than commercial solvers.
Dynamic Adaptation to Spot Market Arbitrage: Handles extreme volatility in spot market electricity pricing and on-site wind generation, cutting energy costs by up to 50% compared to manual scheduling.
Advanced State Feature Representation: Utilizing attention mechanisms and KAN neural architectures enables agents to capture long-range non-linear spatial-temporal interactions without information loss.
3.4.3 Weaknesses
Opaque "Black-Box" Policy Networks: Deep neural policies cannot provide transparent mathematical proofs for their choices, leading to skepticism and rejection by plant operators.
Reward Engineering Bottlenecks & Sample Inefficiency: Designing hand-crafted reward functions that balance production throughput, quality penalties, and energy costs is labor-intensive and prone to exploratory policy collapse.
3.4.4 Opportunities
LLM-Assisted Automated Reward Design: Utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) with few-shot ROSES prompt engineering to automatically design and refine DRL reward functions from human feedback.
Multi-Agent Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE): Distributing control across equipment-level agents (charging, heating, auxiliary cooling) while using a centrally trained attention critic to maintain policy stability.
3.4.5 Risks
Exploratory Out-of-Distribution Policy Failure: DRL policies deployed in unencountered industrial scenarios can generate illegal control actions or violate critical process safety boundaries.
3.5 Cluster 5: Trustworthy Explainable AI & Human-Centric Industry 5.0
3.5.1 Fundamental Philosophy
This paradigm asserts that no AI optimization system—regardless of its mathematical elegance or speed—will be successfully adopted on the shop floor if plant operators do not trust it or if it threatens process safety. Moving beyond pure Industry 4.0 automation, this school operationalizes Industry 5.0 and Intelligence Augmentation (IA). It focuses on opening black-box algorithms through intrinsic interpretable models (decision tree extraction for Genetic Algorithms), post-hoc attributions (SHAP/LIME), multi-objective counterfactual recourse, and smartwatch worker fatigue tracking to create transparent, human-in-the-loop decision environments.
3.5.2 Strengths
High Operator Trust & System Adoption: Providing clear visual and textual explanations (decision tree paths, SHAP force plots, counterfactual recourse) drastically increases operator understandability and acceptance of AI schedules.
Process Safety Governance: Replaces fully autonomous "AI-in-the-loop" systems with Intelligence Augmentation (IA / Human-on-the-loop) frameworks, aligning control actions with Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA) standards.
Actionable Recourse: Counterfactual explanations show managers the exact minimal operational changes required to achieve target makespans or resolve unsat constraints.
3.5.3 Weaknesses
Accuracy-Explainability Trade-off: Highly interpretable intrinsic models (such as shallow decision trees or linear rules) often exhibit lower predictive accuracy compared to complex deep neural networks.
Cognitive Overload for Human Operators: Presenting excessive feature attributions or high-dimensional explanation graphs can overwhelm operators during time-critical production disruptions.
3.5.4 Opportunities
System-Level Multi-Objective Counterfactuals: Utilizing NSGA-II to generate Pareto-optimal counterfactual recourse that balances schedule proximity with makespan improvement.
Dynamic Break Integration (DBI): Coupling Wearable IIoT biometrics with control room XAI interfaces to adjust production schedules dynamically based on real-time operator fatigue.
3.5.5 Risks
Illusion of Control & Biased Overrides: If XAI explanations are poorly calibrated, operators may suffer from automation bias or incorrectly override optimal AI schedules based on flawed human intuition.
4. Competing Approaches
Below is a detailed analysis comparing alternative solution paths across key industrial domains.
4.1 Furnace Scheduling
Bilinear Continuous Optimal Control Path: Models furnace thermodynamics using bilinear differential equations. Applying Pontryagin's Minimum Principle proves that the idle energy function is concave, transforming fixed-order scheduling into finding the shortest path on a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) in polynomial time.
No-Idle Parallel Machine Path: Formulates furnace scheduling as a parallel machine problem with no-idle constraints (Pm, NI | r_j, q_j | C_max). Prohibits empty operational gaps between batches to avoid furnace standby energy waste.
5D Digital Twin & ALTS Search Path: Constructs a 5-Dimensional Digital Twin with a Three-Stage Model (TSM) to track slab logistics with less than 0.98% relative error, using Adaptive Large Neighborhood Tabu Search (ALTS-DT) to assign slabs and minimize makespan.
Deterministic Online Competitive Path: Models online slab arrivals subject to proportional-linear thermal deterioration. Applies online algorithms (DLDR, DLUEC) with proven competitive ratios (1 + 1 / (B * alpha_min)) to minimize residence times in real time.
4.2 Production Optimization
Mathematical Programming & Benders' Decomposition: Formulates hot strip mill scheduling as a Robust Optimization problem, using Benders' decomposition to solve master and sub-problems under rolling time uncertainty.
Multi-Objective Metaheuristic Search: Translates rolling jump penalties and power consumption into Open Multi-Objective TSP (OMOTSP) formulations, solved via SA-MOPSO, EMBO, or GWO.
Integrated IPPS with Deep-Q-Networks: Performs Integrated Process Planning and Scheduling (IPPS) using Asset Administration Shells (AAS) and DQN, allowing dynamic process re-planning without full model re-training.
4.3 Energy Efficiency
Bilinear Idle Energy Function Path: Focuses on continuous optimal control laws during machine idle gaps, switching power to zero and reheating at the last mathematically calculated instant.
Fuzzy Batch Optimization Path: Minimizes natural gas consumption and total weighted tardiness under fuzzy heating values of Blast Furnace Gas (BFG) and Coke Oven Gas (COG) using NSGA-II.
Demand Response & Electricity Spot Market Arbitrage: Formulates Electric Arc Furnace (EAF) and heavy industrial power consumption as a POMDP, using DRL (SAC, MAPPO) to shift load automatically into low-cost electricity pricing windows.
By-Product Gas Network Rolling Horizon Control: Uses adaptive time-series forecasting (ARIMA / Holt-Winters) within a rolling horizon MILP to balance BFG/COG/LDG gas holders and eliminate stack flaring losses.
4.4 Reinforcement Learning
Model-Free Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) with ALADIN: Integrates SAC DRL with Augmented Lagrangian based ALADIN distributed optimization to solve non-convex energy flow models 100 times faster than commercial solvers.
POMDP Evolutionary Search (ES-HP): Models EAF plant demand response as a POMDP with attention mechanisms to capture observation history, optimizing neural policies via population-based evolutionary search.
Multi-Agent MAPPO with Centralized Attention: Implements MAPPO with Centralized Training Decentralized Execution (CTDE) and scaled dot-product attention in the central critic to manage shiftable/controllable industrial loads.
Generative AutoRL with KAN Policy Networks: Uses LLM few-shot ROSES prompting to automate reward design from human feedback, paired with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) as policy actors.
4.5 Digital Twins
5D Walking Beam Reheating Twin: Focuses on high-fidelity physical-virtual mapping of parallel walking beam furnaces using Three-Stage Models (TSM) for charging, stepping, and extraction operations.
Cross-Process IIoT "Data Continent" Twin: Connects Hot Strip Rolling (HSR) and Cold Strip Rolling (CSR) lines into a centralized data center, using IlightGBM (R2 = 0.99) and Three Population Algorithms (TPA) for multi-stand tension control.
Service-Oriented AAS Digital Twin: Implements type-3 Asset Administration Shells (AAS) using BaSyx middleware to provide standardized submodels for live Integrated Process Planning and Scheduling (IPPS).
Human-Centric Smartwatch Twin: Extends Digital Twin shop-floor models to ingest smartwatch operator biometrics, implementing Dynamic Break Integration (DBI) for Industry 5.0 worker fatigue tracking.
4.6 Explainable AI (XAI)
Intrinsic Decision Tree Extraction: Extracts explicit decision tree rules from Genetic Algorithm selection, crossover, and mutation mechanisms to make evolutionary scheduling fully transparent.
Post-Hoc Feature Attributions (SHAP/LIME): Decomposes deep neural network or MARL control actions into SHAP force plots to show operators the exact feature contributions behind order dispatching decisions.
System-Level Multi-Objective Counterfactuals: Uses multi-objective NSGA-II to generate Pareto-optimal counterfactual recourse, presenting operators with actionable operational modifications.
Trustworthy Assessment Standards: Adapts ALTAI European guidelines and metrics (simplicity, fidelity, actionability) to evaluate transparency in planning and scheduling tools.
4.7 Industrial Automation
Pyramidal Automation Hierarchy: Classical 5-level automation pyramid (L1/L2 control to MES/ERP) operating with restricted data exchange and manual rescheduling.
Holonic Multi-Agent Virtual Markets: Breaks the automation pyramid by establishing agent-based cross-level communication, using virtual market auctions to re-allocate off-spec products in sub-seconds.
Intelligence Augmentation (IA) & Process Safety 4.0: Replaces fully automated AI with Human-in-the-Loop (HiL) and Human-on-the-Loop (HoL) architectures, aligning control actions with Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA) safety layers.
5. Key Trade-Offs
5.1 Reliability versus Adaptability
A central tension exists between rigid, mathematically provable schedules and flexible, highly adaptive control policies.
Exact Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) models and robust optimization frameworks deliver maximum reliability: they guarantee constraint satisfaction, respect physical safety margins, and yield deterministic performance bounds. However, this reliability comes at the expense of adaptability. When unexpected real-time disruptions occur—such as random machine breakdowns, abrupt weather shifts affecting renewable output, or sudden order changes—rigid mathematical schedules can become infeasible, requiring time-consuming re-optimization.
Conversely, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Multi-Agent Systems offer extreme adaptability: they execute sub-second online inference and dynamically adjust load profiles under spot market price volatility. Yet, this adaptability compromises reliability. DRL policies operate without formal mathematical convergence proofs during online execution and can exhibit out-of-distribution failures when encountering unlearned plant states, posing operational risks to high-temperature metallurgical equipment.
5.2 Optimization versus Explainability
The literature demonstrates a direct structural trade-off between predictive/computational performance and model interpretability.
High-capacity, non-linear models—such as Deep Neural Networks, Soft Actor-Critic DRL agents, and IlightGBM gradient boosters—achieve superior optimization performance (e.g., predicting rolling forces with R2 = 0.99 or reducing spot market energy costs by over 50%). However, these architectures operate as opaque "black boxes." Their decision logic cannot be intuitively audited by control room supervisors, creating a barrier to shop-floor adoption.
On the other hand, highly explainable models—such as decision trees, shallow rule-based heuristics, or linear programming formulations—provide complete transparency, clear causal justifications, and easy auditing. However, their simplicity prevents them from capturing complex, non-linear physical interactions across multi-stand rolling mills or multi-zone gas networks, resulting in lower predictive accuracy and suboptimal energy savings.
5.3 Innovation versus Implementation Risk
Bridging frontier AI research with real-world heavy industrial plants involves balancing technological innovation against catastrophic operational risk.
Cutting-edge innovations—such as LLM-assisted reward engineering (ROSES prompts), Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), 5D Digital Twins, and multi-agent attention mechanisms—offer transformative operational efficiency gains. However, their implementation risk in primary metals manufacturing is high. A failure in an autonomous AI controller managing a 1200°C reheating furnace, an Electric Arc Furnace, or a high-speed tandem cold rolling mill can cause catastrophic equipment damage, severe metal scrap losses, or worker fatalities.
Consequently, plant managers frequently favor conservative, incremental innovations—such as rule-based heuristics, static safety buffers, or offline simulation evaluation—accepting higher energy costs to guarantee process stability and safety compliance.
5.4 Automation versus Human Control
The corpus exposes a philosophical shift regarding the role of human workers in digitalized manufacturing: the conflict between Industry 4.0 full automation and Industry 5.0 human-centric control.
The full automation paradigm (Industry 4.0) seeks to eliminate human intervention from the decision loop, replacing human schedulers with autonomous multi-agent DRL policies or automated Basic Process Control Systems (BPCS). Proponents argue that automated systems execute decisions faster, process high-dimensional IIoT sensor streams without cognitive bias, and operate continuously without fatigue.
In contrast, the human-centric paradigm (Industry 5.0 / Intelligence Augmentation) asserts that fully automated AI lacks socio-emotional intelligence, contextual awareness, and holistic situational understanding. Proponents demonstrate that augmenting operators with XAI recourse tools and integrating wearable smartwatches to track worker fatigue (Dynamic Break Integration) yields superior operational stability—reducing cycle time variance by 56% while preserving process safety and worker well-being.
6. Divergent Insights
6.1 Contrast 1: Modeling Furnace Dynamics — Static Machine Modes vs. Continuous Bilinear Physics
A fundamental disagreement exists between classical operations research literature and modern optimal control approaches regarding how industrial furnaces should be modeled.
The Static Mode School: Traditional scheduling models simplify furnace behavior into discrete operational modes (e.g., "ON", "OFF", "STANDBY") connected by a static transition graph with constant power/time penalties.
The Continuous Physics School: Benedikt et al. argue that static mode graphs are overly restrictive and inaccurate for heat-intensive furnaces. They prove that modeling true continuous bilinear dynamics using Pontryagin's Minimum Principle reveals a concave idle energy function, enabling exact optimal control laws (switching to zero power and reheating at the last mathematically calculated instant) that achieve significantly higher energy savings than static mode approximations.
6.2 Contrast 2: Algorithmic Execution — Offline MILP Optimization vs. Sub-Second Online DRL
The literature reflects a sharp divide over how to solve online scheduling problems subject to dynamic electricity spot market pricing.
The Mathematical Programming View: Assumes scheduling problems must be solved using exact MILP or robust optimization with rolling horizon frameworks to guarantee constraint satisfaction and lower bounds.
The Deep Reinforcement Learning View: Shah et al. and Wang et al. demonstrate that online MILP solvers stall or scale poorly when handling industrial-sized POMDP formulations under real-time price and wind generation volatility. They prove that DRL agents trained offline execute online decisions in milliseconds via feed-forward inference, achieving total energy costs competitive with theoretical MILP benchmarks while running over 100 times faster.
6.3 Contrast 3: System Architecture — Centralized Monolithic Control vs. Decentralized Multi-Agent Auction Markets
Authors diverge on the architectural design required for dynamic rescheduling and off-spec product reallocation.
Centralized Optimization: Formulates plant-wide scheduling as a single, monolithic master problem (e.g., CMOP or OMOTSP) solved by a centralized algorithm.
Decentralized Multi-Agent Auctions: Neuer et al. argue that centralized automation pyramids (ERP/MES) cannot process real-time off-spec product disruptions across plant boundaries. They propose a holonic multi-agent system (I2MSteel) where product and order agents participate in virtual market auctions, using predicted post-processing state windows to re-allocate failed steel coils in sub-seconds.
6.4 Contrast 4: Explainability Paradigm — Intrinsic Interpretable Models vs. Post-Hoc Feature Attributions
A technical debate exists regarding how to achieve transparency in AI-assisted scheduling.
The Intrinsic School: Wang & Chen contend that post-hoc explanations on opaque models fail to capture true decision logic. They propose intrinsic XAI methods—extracting explicit decision trees and dynamic transformation diagrams directly from Genetic Algorithm operations—to provide standardized, structurally transparent explanations.
The Post-Hoc & Counterfactual School: Theumer et al. and Mehdiyev et al. argue that restricting industrial AI to intrinsically simple models sacrifices predictive and optimization performance. They advocate pairing high-capacity deep MARL or gradient boosting models with post-hoc SHAP/LIME attributions or system-level NSGA-II counterfactual recourse, giving operators actionable recourse without compromising model accuracy.
6.5 Contrast 5: Industrial Governance — Fully Autonomous AI vs. Human-Centric Intelligence Augmentation (IA)
A strategic disagreement emerges regarding the ultimate governance goal of industrial AI deployment.
Autonomous AI Governance: Focuses on developing fully autonomous Cyber-Physical Production Systems where AI agents make and execute closed-loop scheduling decisions with minimal human intervention.
Intelligence Augmentation & Safety Governance: Arunthavanathan et al. and Javaid & Ullah prove that fully automated AI lacks socio-emotional context and presents severe process safety risks under unmodeled industrial disturbances. They argue that AI must be restricted to Intelligence Augmentation (IA / Human-in-the-Loop), pairing AI computational speed with human expert judgment, smartwatch fatigue monitoring, and LOPA safety compliance.

MASTER PROMPT - DOCUMENT ANALYSIS AND ORGANIZATIONAL SYNTHESIS
Role
Act as a senior research analyst and academic writer specialising in industrial operations, steel manufacturing, energy-efficient production, operations research, artificial intelligence, reinforcement learning, Digital Twins, explainable AI and responsible industrial automation. Combine rigorous academic analysis with a management-oriented perspective. All conclusions must be evidence-based, traceable and critically validated.
Course context
This assignment belongs to Managing with Artificial Intelligence in the Master's Degree in Industrial Organisation Engineering at Universidad Politecnica de Madrid. The course focuses on the applied, critical and responsible use of AI as a cognitive assistant for managerial decision-making. The work must show problem structuring, an effective AI-assisted workflow, validation against original sources, identification of errors and limitations, human oversight and a professionally defensible result.
Organisational scenario
An industrial organisation seeks to reduce operational complexity, improve energy efficiency and deploy intelligent automation in a high-stakes environment, particularly steelmaking, furnace operation and production scheduling. A former engineer compiled 31 academic and technical documents, but the knowledge remains fragmented. The organisation needs an initial, controlled and navigable knowledge base.
Assignment
Complete Document Analysis and Organizational Synthesis - Task 1: Inventory and Initial Scan. First, extract and validate titles, authors, publication sources, dates, keywords and concise initial snippets. Second, determine and explain the boundaries of the knowledge domain. Begin the narrative by acknowledging the complexity of the industrial problem and defining the analytical and AI-supported tools brought to it. This is an inventory and initial scan, not a definitive technology-selection recommendation.
Input and source control
You will receive 31 research documents, the assignment image and the course syllabus. Treat the 31 documents as the evidence base and the other two files only as instructions. Create a manifest, assign D01-D31, check readability, detect duplicates and confirm a 31/31 corpus. Stop and identify missing files if the count cannot be verified. If platform limits require batching, use one extraction schema and consolidate all batches before synthesis.
Evidence extraction protocol
Do not rely only on filenames or abstracts. For every source, inspect the first page, abstract, keywords, stated objective, method, application, results, conclusion and limitations where available. Record exact title, authors, year, venue, DOI, keywords, industrial process, research problem, objective, model, performance criteria, case or data, main findings, quantitative results, limitations, relevance and a 40-70 word evidence-grounded snippet. Write Not reported when a field cannot be verified; never guess metadata.
Domain structure to test
Use the following only as a provisional hypothesis: steel production scheduling and coordination; energy-aware and sustainable production; dynamic, online and robust scheduling; optimisation and intelligent decision methods; digital infrastructure and real-time support; and explainability, safety and human-centred governance. Permit one primary and several secondary themes. Revise the taxonomy when the documents support a better structure.
Domain boundaries
Define the core domain, industrial processes, operational decisions, performance dimensions, methods, time horizons and human-AI roles. Separate core, enabling and peripheral topics. State inclusion and exclusion criteria, and identify underrepresented or absent areas. Classify production scheduling, furnace operations, energy management, uncertainty, optimisation, prediction, reinforcement learning, Digital Twins, IoT, XAI, human oversight, safety and LLMs as core, enabling or peripheral based on evidence.
Analytical requirements
Do not produce 31 isolated summaries. Compare recurring problems, variables, constraints, objectives and methods; connect prediction, optimisation and control; compare static, dynamic, online and real-time approaches; distinguish conventional optimisation from learning-based methods; assess real implementation versus simulation; and analyse explainability, safety and human control. Mark content as extracted evidence, cross-document synthesis, analyst inference or unknown when appropriate.
Required output
Prepare a polished Word-ready report in formal academic English with: cover page; executive summary; organisational context and problem definition; AI-assisted methodology; a complete 31-row metadata inventory; a second analytical scan matrix; domain boundaries; hierarchical topic map; connected thematic synthesis; gaps, tensions and limitations; management relevance and next steps; validation and responsible AI; an AI-use statement; conclusions; APA references; and a coverage checklist.
Evidence rules
Use APA-style citations and add page numbers for specific results where possible. Verify every numerical result against the source. Do not invent authors, years, venues, DOIs, methods or findings. Do not use external sources unless explicitly authorised. Paraphrase rather than copy. Do not present simulation as proven plant performance or a proposed framework as deployed unless the source confirms it. Keep conclusions within the evidence.
Writing requirements
Write in English, with precise and readable academic language, numbered headings, consistent terminology and purposeful tables. Define abbreviations at first use. Avoid generic AI history, repetition and inflated claims. Make the report understandable without opening every paper. If file creation is supported, produce an editable DOCX.
Final quality gate

Part II  Task 1 Inventory and Initial Scan
1 Executive summary
Steel production scheduling is a coupled decision problem in which equipment capacity, metallurgical constraints, delivery performance, energy use, uncertain disturbances and safety interact. The 31-document corpus does not describe one isolated algorithm; it maps an emerging decision architecture that combines mathematical optimisation, forecasting, simulation, reinforcement learning, Digital Twins and human oversight.
The central knowledge domain is intelligent, energy-aware production scheduling for steel and other heat-intensive manufacturing processes. Furnace and rolling operations form the industrial core. Dynamic rescheduling, energy-system coordination and multi-objective optimisation extend that core. Prediction, Deep Reinforcement Learning, Digital Twins, IoT and explainability are enabling layers. Generic job-shop, forging, aluminium and process-safety studies sit at the periphery but provide transferable methods.
The strongest recurring conclusion is that no single objective or method is sufficient. Energy, makespan, tardiness, stability, quality and safety must be considered together. Mathematical models provide explicit constraints and auditability; metaheuristics provide scalability; forecasting and Digital Twins introduce current information; learning methods reduce online computation; and XAI plus human-in-the-loop design address trust and responsibility. Evidence of industrial deployment exists, but much of the corpus remains simulation- or case-study-based, limiting direct comparison and generalisation.
2 Organisational context and problem definition
The organisation seeks to reduce operational complexity, improve energy efficiency and introduce intelligent automation in a high-stakes steel-production environment. The immediate task is not to select a final scheduling system. It is to convert a fragmented document archive into a controlled knowledge base that shows what problems, processes, objectives, methods and governance issues the literature actually covers.
Task 1 therefore has two outputs: a verified inventory of all 31 documents and an initial synthesis that defines the domain boundaries. The intended users are operations managers, production planners, energy managers, industrial engineers and technical decision-makers who need to understand both operational opportunities and implementation risks.
Success is defined by complete source coverage, accurate metadata, evidence-linked snippets, a defensible taxonomy and explicit limitations. The scan supports later model comparison and implementation design, but it does not establish that any reported algorithm will transfer unchanged to another plant.
3 AI-assisted analysis methodology
The analysis used a general-purpose generative AI assistant as a cognitive aid for document parsing, metadata consolidation, thematic coding and cross-document synthesis. The workflow retained the original PDFs as the evidence base and used the syllabus and assignment image only to frame the deliverable.
Corpus control: the research set was separated from the syllabus and checked for 31 unique readable PDFs.
Metadata extraction: first pages, publication details, abstracts and keywords were inspected and normalised into a common schema.
Evidence extraction: objectives, methods, application settings, reported results and relevant limitations were taken from the articles rather than inferred from filenames.
Thematic coding: every document received one primary theme for corpus-level counting and secondary conceptual links for synthesis.
Cross-document synthesis: findings were compared by operational problem, objective, uncertainty treatment, decision method, data architecture and human-control model.
Validation: quantitative claims highlighted in the narrative were rechecked against the relevant source passages. Ambiguous bibliographic details were not reconstructed from guesswork.
This procedure improves consistency and speed, but it does not eliminate extraction error or interpretive bias. The resulting report requires final student review, particularly for citation formatting and any claims that will be defended orally.

6 Boundaries of the knowledge domain
6.1 Domain definition
The corpus defines the domain as the design and governance of data-informed decision systems for scheduling, coordinating and controlling steel and heat-intensive production, with particular attention to furnace operations, rolling processes, energy performance and uncertainty.
6.2 Inclusion criteria
Operational allocation, sequencing, timing, batching, rescheduling or resource-coordination decisions.
Steelmaking, continuous casting, reheating, rolling, heat treatment, ladle logistics or closely transferable heat-intensive production.
Objectives involving energy, cost, makespan, tardiness, throughput, stability, quality or safety.
Mathematical optimisation, heuristics, forecasting, simulation, machine learning, reinforcement learning, Digital Twins or agent-based decision support.
Explainability, human oversight or process-safety work that governs industrial AI decisions.
6.3 Exclusion criteria
Pure furnace or metallurgical design without a scheduling, control or decision-support contribution.
Generic AI research with no transferable production-planning or industrial-governance relevance.
Maintenance, quality inspection or supply-chain topics that do not affect the defined operational decision system.

8 Cross-document thematic synthesis
8.1 Scheduling is a coupled multi-objective problem
The literature consistently treats scheduling as a compromise among production and energy objectives rather than a single sequencing problem. Furnace studies minimise idle energy, residence time or working time (Benedikt et al., 2021, D01; Rao & Zhang, 2025, D15; Xu et al., 2024, D23), while integrated models connect furnace schedules to rolling plans, ladle dispatching or delivery performance (Han et al., 2020, D12; Wang et al., 2022, D17; Gomes et al., 2021, D22).
The reported improvements demonstrate potential but are not directly comparable. Han et al. report 1.21% lower energy use at constant production efficiency (D12); Gomes et al. report reductions up to 13% in energy cost and 90% in tardiness (D22); and Hidri et al. report 29.57% lower energy consumption with a 0.12% makespan increase (D31). These values arise from different systems, baselines and objective definitions.
8.2 Uncertainty changes the scheduling architecture
Static schedules become fragile when release times, breakdowns, processing times or energy flows are uncertain. The corpus responds through proactive schedules (D02), forecast-informed robust rescheduling (D03), fuzzy representations (D07), rolling-horizon control (D24), disturbance-specific policies (D18) and robust optimisation (D28). The common architectural pattern is to sense or estimate uncertainty, quantify its operational effect, and trigger an appropriately scaled adjustment rather than repeatedly rebuilding the full schedule.
8.3 Methods trade transparency for scale and speed
MILP and exact algorithms make constraints and objectives explicit, but large industrial instances motivate decomposition, heuristics and metaheuristics. Matheuristics combine both properties, as in the MILP-seeded variable-neighbourhood search of D22. DRL and MARL shift computation toward offline training and offer fast online decisions (D05, D09, D21), but their learned policies are harder to verify and can depend strongly on reward design and training scenarios.
The LLM-assisted framework in D20 is therefore important but peripheral: it uses human feedback and prompting to help design DRL rewards, rather than replacing the scheduler with a language model. This distinction prevents an unsupported interpretation of generative AI as the operational optimisation engine.
8.4 Digital Twins connect models to current plant state
Digital Twins and IoT address the gap between a mathematically valid schedule and the plant state in which it must be executed. The furnace twin in D10 estimates slab positions and operation times with reported relative error below 0.98%. D19 connects hot- and cold-rolling data, while D26 and D30 use digital representations to update scheduling decisions. The corpus nevertheless uses the term Digital Twin at different maturity levels, from simulation-supported planning to live, bidirectional decision support.
8.5 Explainability and human control are operational requirements
XAI papers broaden performance beyond solution quality. D04 adapts explanation techniques to genetic algorithms; D08 produces system-aware counterfactuals; and D13 combines MARL with SHAP, reporting average reward improvements of 22% over FIFO and 15% over SSTN across 52 simulated episodes. D06 and D25 show why explanations must be meaningful to users and embedded in governance, not added only as post-hoc visualisations.
The human-centred contribution in D16 and the process-safety argument in D25 indicate that full autonomy is not the default target. In a high-stakes steel environment, the stronger model is decision augmentation: AI proposes, predicts or optimises; authorised personnel review exceptions, safety constraints and consequences.
9 Gaps tensions and limitations
Comparability: studies use different plants, horizons, objective functions, baselines and definitions of energy, so headline percentages cannot be ranked directly.
Validation depth: several contributions rely on simulation, synthetic instances or one case plant. Longitudinal multi-site evidence is limited.
Data readiness: many models assume accurate timestamps, process states or forecasts, while data quality, interoperability and ownership receive less attention.
Human factors: explainability and human-centred scheduling are present but remain a smaller branch than algorithmic optimisation.
Governance and safety: cybersecurity, fallback modes, authority to override, audit trails and model-change control are not systematically integrated into the scheduling models.
Sustainability scope: energy or cost is often used as a proxy for sustainability; lifecycle emissions and marginal carbon intensity are less consistently modelled.
Transferability: adjacent studies in job shops, forging, casting and aluminium are methodologically useful but cannot be treated as direct evidence for a steel furnace without adaptation.
10 Management relevance and next analytical steps
The initial scan suggests a modular decision architecture rather than one universal algorithm. A practical organisation should separate data capture, forecasting, optimisation, simulation or Digital Twin validation, explanation and human approval. This makes it possible to improve one layer without treating the entire system as an opaque autonomous controller.
The next phase should construct a comparison matrix for candidate approaches using plant-specific criteria: decision horizon, processes covered, objectives, data required, computational latency, uncertainty handling, explainability, integration effort, safety controls and evidence of deployment. The organisation should then select a bounded pilot, define a baseline and establish acceptance criteria before live use.
Map the actual steel process, decisions and constraints against the domain taxonomy.
Audit data availability, quality, latency and system interfaces.
Select a narrow decision problem with measurable energy and service KPIs.
Benchmark a transparent optimisation baseline before adding DRL or other learning methods.
Use simulation or a Digital Twin for shadow-mode testing and stress scenarios.
Design explanations, override rules, logging and escalation responsibilities with operators.
Evaluate performance over time and across disturbances before any increase in autonomy.
11 Validation and responsible use of AI
AI supported document extraction, normalisation, classification and drafting. Source-level checks were used for bibliographic information and the numerical results highlighted in the report. The tool was not treated as an independent authority, and no external web sources were added to the evidence base.
Residual risks include PDF extraction errors, differences between online-first and issue dates, oversimplification in short snippets and interpretive bias in the primary-theme assignment. Cross-document synthesis is an analytical interpretation; it should not be mistaken for a conclusion stated identically by all authors.
For responsible use in the course, the prompt and workflow are disclosed, the source set is enumerated, and the final student remains responsible for accuracy, citation quality and oral defence. For responsible industrial use, confidential plant data, role-based access, override authority, audit logging and safe fallback procedures would need to be defined before deployment.
12 Conclusions
The 31 documents collectively describe a transition from isolated, deterministic production schedules toward connected decision systems that integrate energy, uncertainty, current plant information and human responsibility. The operational centre of the corpus is steel and furnace scheduling; optimisation remains the dominant decision mechanism, while forecasting, DRL, Digital Twins and XAI expand adaptability and usability.
The knowledge base is sufficiently coherent to support a second-stage comparative review, but not yet a final technology decision. The most defensible next move is to define a plant-specific use case and evaluate candidate architectures against both operational KPIs and governance requirements.

Part I  Submitted prompt
The following prompt defines the evidence controls, coding rules, graph semantics and validation requirements used to produce Task 2. It is designed for a general-purpose AI system with document-reading capability.
MASTER PROMPT - TASK 2 TOPOGRAPHICAL MAPPING
Role
Act as a senior research analyst specialising in industrial operations, steel manufacturing, energy-aware production scheduling, operations research, artificial intelligence, Digital Twins, explainable AI and knowledge mapping. Work as both an evidence analyst and an information architect. Produce a defensible map of the supplied literature rather than a decorative diagram.
Course and assignment context
This work belongs to Managing with Artificial Intelligence in the Master's Degree in Industrial Organisation Engineering at Universidad Politecnica de Madrid. The course assesses problem formulation, AI-assisted workflow design, validation, traceability, professional judgement and responsible use of AI. Task 2 is titled Topographical Mapping. It requires a hierarchical topic tree and a cross-reference network graph in order to identify where knowledge is concentrated, where it is isolated and which structural relationships are hidden by document-by-document reading.
Evidence base
Use the same verified corpus of 31 research documents analysed in Task 1. Treat the task image and syllabus as instructions, not scientific evidence. Assign stable identifiers D01-D31 and ensure that every document appears in the mapping. Do not introduce external sources unless expressly authorised.
Objective
Transform the 31-document inventory into a transparent knowledge topology. The final result must show: the hierarchy of the domain; the thematic position of every source; connections among topics; dense knowledge clusters; bridge themes; weak or isolated areas; and the practical meaning of the structure for an industrial organisation considering AI-supported steel scheduling.
Coding procedure
Read the title, abstract, objective, method, case, results and conclusions of each paper. Code each document against a controlled theme dictionary. Allow multiple tags because papers can connect operational problems, objectives, technologies and governance. Record a clear reason for each tag. Distinguish author-provided keywords from analyst-assigned themes.
Hierarchical topic tree
Create a top-down tree with one root domain and no more than five first-level branches. Use the following provisional branches only as a starting hypothesis: industrial processes and scheduling; performance objectives; decision and optimisation methods; digital infrastructure and live decision support; and governance and human responsibility. Add meaningful second-level topics and attach source IDs to the relevant leaves. Revise the hierarchy when the evidence supports a better structure. Avoid duplicate branches with different labels.
Cross-reference network
Build a reproducible thematic co-occurrence network. Theme nodes must represent analyst-assigned topics. Connect two theme nodes when they co-occur in at least one document. Set edge weight equal to the number of documents in which the two themes co-occur. Set node size according to the number of documents tagged with the theme. Display strong relationships clearly and retain emerging one-document links when they reveal isolation. State explicitly that this is a thematic cross-reference network, not a bibliographic citation network.
Quantitative analysis
Calculate the frequency and percentage of documents assigned to every theme. Because multi-label coding is used, percentages are not mutually exclusive and do not sum to 100%. Rank the strongest co-occurrences. Identify the dense core, bridge themes, peripheral clusters and emerging islands. Do not equate frequency with quality, importance or industrial readiness.
Interpretation requirements
Explain the structural meaning of the maps. Identify relationships among scheduling, energy, mathematical optimisation, uncertainty, real-time decision-making, forecasting, reinforcement learning, Digital Twins, explainability, human-centred design and process safety. Highlight where advanced optimisation is weakly connected to explainability or human oversight. Separate evidence from analyst interpretation and avoid causal claims not supported by the corpus.

Prepare an editable Word report in formal academic English containing: cover page; the complete prompt used; executive summary; mapping methodology; coding dictionary; hierarchical topic tree; cross-reference network graph; theme-concentration analysis; source-to-theme matrix; analysis of dense, bridging and isolated knowledge; hidden structural relationships; managerial implications; limitations and validation; AI-use statement; conclusions; and an appendix mapping all 31 source IDs to titles and assigned themes.

Use restrained colours consistently across all figures. Include figure captions and explain each visual in the surrounding text. Do not use a network graphic as a substitute for analysis.

Verify numerical counts programmatically or by an independent recount. Explain modelling choices, including the theme dictionary and edge definition. Report ambiguous classifications and acknowledge that thematic coding involves analyst judgement.
Writing requirements

Lead with the structural conclusion, use numbered headings, distinguish evidence from interpretation and connect the maps to managerial action. Avoid generic descriptions of AI. Keep the final claims within the supplied evidence.

1 Executive summary
The corpus has a dense operational core and a much thinner governance perimeter. Scheduling and coordination appears in 27 of 31 documents, mathematical optimisation in 19 and energy in 18. These three themes form the strongest triangle in the network. Real-time decision-making and uncertainty connect this core to Digital Twins, forecasting and reinforcement learning.
The maps also expose a structural imbalance. Explainability appears in five documents, human-centricity and safety in six, and LLM-assisted optimisation in only one. The explainability and human-safety cluster is connected mainly to generic planning and scheduling studies rather than to the most energy-intensive steel optimisation models. The main knowledge gap is therefore not another scheduling algorithm, but the integration of advanced operational optimisation with explanations, human authority, safety and deployment governance.
The network is a thematic co-occurrence graph, not a bibliographic citation network. Its edges show that two themes were assigned to the same source; they do not prove that one paper cites or influences another.

8 Hidden structural relationships
An operational core dominates the field. Scheduling, mathematical optimisation and energy form the central triangle. The literature primarily asks how to produce a better schedule and then how to solve that schedule at industrial scale.
Real-time capability is the principal bridge. RT connects uncertainty to Digital Twins and reinforcement learning. This suggests that dynamic information and decision latency, rather than algorithm novelty alone, drive the transition from planning models to operational systems.
Digital Twins are an enabling layer, not a separate objective. DT co-occurs with scheduling in all seven DT-tagged documents and with real-time decisions in six. Its role is to supply state, synchronisation and validation for decision methods.
Prediction usually feeds optimisation. ML connects most strongly to scheduling and mathematical optimisation and then to uncertainty and real-time decisions. The typical pattern is forecast or predict first, optimise or reschedule second.
Governance is structurally separated from energy optimisation. The HC-XA link is supported by four documents, yet the corpus contains no direct HC-EN co-occurrence under this coding. Human authority, safety and wellbeing are therefore not integrated into the main energy-optimisation cluster.
Explainable autonomy remains rare. Only one document directly connects reinforcement learning and explainability, and only one connects explainability with real-time decision-making. The most autonomous methods are therefore not yet matched by an equally dense explanation literature.
LLM use is emerging and narrowly defined. D20 uses an LLM to assist reward design through human feedback. The source does not establish LLMs as direct plant schedulers, and the map provides no basis for treating that method as mature industrial practice.

10 Managerial implications
The knowledge map supports a layered implementation strategy. The organisation should not select a Digital Twin, reinforcement-learning agent or optimisation algorithm in isolation. It should define the operational decision, performance trade-offs, uncertainty sources, data layer and human-control model together.
1.  Begin with the dense evidence core: a bounded scheduling problem with explicit energy and delivery KPIs.
2.  Use forecasting or a Digital Twin only where current information changes the decision and can be supplied reliably.
3.  Benchmark advanced learning methods against a transparent mathematical or rule-based baseline.
4.  Add explanation, override and escalation requirements before increasing autonomy.
5.  Treat the isolated topics as research and pilot priorities rather than as mature off-the-shelf capabilities.
6.  Update the map as new sources or plant evidence become available so that the topology remains a decision aid rather than a static figure.
11 Limitations validation and responsible AI
The maps depend on a controlled coding scheme created for this assignment. A different analyst could split or merge themes, and frequency can be influenced by the composition of the supplied corpus. The network captures co-occurrence, not citation direction, causal influence, research quality or implementation readiness.
Validation included a complete D01-D31 matrix, automated theme counts and automated pairwise edge counts. The prompt, coding dictionary and graph semantics are disclosed so that the map can be reproduced or challenged. The figures do not add external evidence and do not infer missing links as facts.
AI assisted source organisation, thematic coding, calculation and drafting. Human review remains necessary because category definitions and the interpretation of structural gaps involve judgement. In an industrial context, the same principle applies: AI can expand analytical capacity but cannot assume responsibility for safety-critical decisions.
12 Conclusions
The topography shows a mature and densely connected body of work around scheduling, optimisation and energy, supported by a growing real-time layer. Digital Twins, forecasting and reinforcement learning are not separate destinations; they are bridges that supply information or fast decisions to the scheduling core.
The most important isolated region is governance. Explainability, human-centred design and process safety remain comparatively small and weakly connected to the energy-optimisation cluster. For a high-stakes steel environment, the next research and implementation priority should be to integrate these governance requirements into the same models and pilots used to pursue operational performance.
